item.title: The Ripple Effect of Going for It
item.description: Can you learn to captain a yacht at 62 and turn it into a world-traveling lifestyle? Absolutely! Below, Sine Maria shares a first-hand account of her family’s latest charter with Dream Yacht in the Balearic Islands. Read on for an inspiring look at courage, partnership, and what happens when you say yes to a new adventure on the water. The Ripple Effect of Going for It On breaking into worlds you weren’t born into, and what happens when you actually do the thing. By: Good Life Designed and Sine Maria If there’s one thing I’ve learned from my mom, it’s that life has so much to offer and the limit of your world is only limited by your ability to keep expanding. In the middle of the pandemic, as part of our collective pause, she and I decided to go through the whole Good Life Designed program together again. It was through that process that she decided she wanted to be closer to nature, swim more, and learn how to sail. She didn’t grow up around sailing, knew it was costly and a bit of a boys club, but always admired the access it gave those who knew how. That hobby could take you anywhere in the world. The world of sailing requires a unique blend of resources, courage, technical education, practice, and willing crew members to go along for the ride and be there while you figure things out on your first trips alone. It thrives behind heavy yacht club doors that some are born with access into – but most don’t even know exist. The dream of being certified as a sailor has an even smaller niche- attracting those who thrive on the pressure to read and respond to the chaos of the elements at sea while holding the responsibility of passengers’ lives in their hands. Now that I have experienced the reward that comes with that kind of responsibility – I see the draw. Breaking Into a World You Weren’t Born Into I tried to look into data about women certified sailors but couldn’t find any credible data because no one seems to be particularly interested in that stat – however I can tell you there aren’t many. Sailing, just due to the nature of it, the time it requires, the unease that comes with the experience, especially as you’re getting your first solo trips under your belt, is enough to send anyone right over the edge. It’s heady, it’s overwhelming, it’s complicated, it’s technical, and it feels uncertain and dangerous before you’re skilled and experienced enough to feel truly comfortable and at ease on the water. When Pernille got the ping to learn to sail, the biggest question was how, as a 62-year-old woman, was she going to do it. She tried visiting yacht clubs but as someone who wasn’t interested in the social component and was really looking for the technical skills to captain her own ship, it didn’t feel like the best place to spend her time or money. The classes and day sail opportunities to get out on the water were nice, but if she really wanted to learn everything she needed to, she needed something different. She came across Nautilus Sailing, a week-long course in the Sea of Cortez that would teach you everything you need to know about sailing and cap off the week with a test that would certify you to sail on your own anywhere in the world. My dad at the time was in the most stressful period of his career, navigating his independent school and their 400 families through Covid. Using his coveted spring break to learn to navigate another set of uncharted territories felt not quite like the vacation he needed. But he took a leap of his own and joined her anyway. They spent a week disconnected from everything to focus on learning the thing that would later give them access to the life they live now – barely imaginable to them then. Heading out on what feel like once-in-a-lifetime week long sailing experiences all over the world with friends and family. In 6 years since becoming certified, have now completed their 15th sail and have endless shared albums to show for it. They’ve sailed all over, eight times in La Paz, Mexico, once i…

item.title: French Polynesia Cabin Cruise: The Floating Boutique Hotel for Effortless Island Hopping
item.description: Imagine waking up in a comfortable suite aboard a premium catamaran. You stretch out on crisp sheets and wonder what spectacular view is awaiting you today. Will it be the majestic twin peaks of Bora Bora or the white sand beaches and tropical jungles of Huahine? You step on deck and sniff the air: today’s port is actually the vanilla-scented shores of Taha’a. That’s what life is like aboard a French Polynesia cabin cruise. Every day, you get to go on a new adventure. At night, you rest and relax in the comfort of a spacious cabin aboard a shared catamaran charter. For many travelers, the freedom to visit multiple destinations rather than be confined to a single resort makes a cabin cruise a much better option than a typical holiday on land. What Is a French Polynesia Cabin Cruise? A French Polynesia catamaran cruise or cabin cruise is a travel option where you book a private cabin with its own attached bathroom on a catamaran. Instead of chartering an entire yacht yourself, you share the vessel with a small group of other travelers. How Cabin Cruises Work The catamaran operates much like a small-scale cruise ship but with a personalized touch. Your captain navigates the islands, and an onboard steward prepares your meals. This vacation style eliminates the stress of trip planning, sailing logistics, and meal preparation. And since vessels are shared among travelers, cabin cruises are more affordable than booking Tahiti yacht charters . Why It Feels Like a Floating Boutique Hotel Unlike massive cruise ships that carry thousands of passengers, a catamaran hosts between 8 and 12 guests. This creates an intimate atmosphere, similar to that of a small hotel, except you also get to experience different destinations and activities every day. In French Polynesia, our cabin cruises are offered on the Bali 5.4, Lagoon 620, and the Fountaine Pajot Ipanema 58, each accommodating 12 guests. Comfort and Convenience: What Is a Cabin Cruise Like Onboard? Life aboard a cabin charter is defined by relaxation and comfort. Your catamaran features decks, shaded outdoor dining areas, and a forward trampoline net. This net is a great spot to lounge as the islands glide by. No jostling for sunbathing space on crowded beaches or lining up to rent gear from stands along the shore. You can get all the sun you want on deck, and the cruise includes the use of water sports equipment. You can step directly off the yacht’s transom steps into the water, swim, snorkel, or kayak to your heart’s content. Island Hopping Without Repacking or Airport Transfers With 118 islands and atolls spread across an area as vast as Western Europe, French Polynesia island hopping is all about discovering the unique character of each destination. However, having your base camp be a hotel or resort limits your options. It also means you have to go through a drawn-out process of getting there before you can visit each different island. Traditional travelers must pack their suitcases, check out of their resorts, take a taxi to the airport, wait in security lines, and fly to the next island, only to repeat the check-in process. Meanwhile, on Tahiti cabin cruises , you unpack your bags once on arrival. While you relax on deck or sleep in your cabin, the catamaran moves you between Tahiti and other destinations like Huahine, Raiatea, Taha’a, and Bora Bora. A Tahiti cabin charter eliminates the need for regional flights and ferry schedules, saving you both travel stress and vacation time. Space, Food, Privacy, and Seasickness: Honest Answers Before booking a sailing trip, it is normal to have a few questions about how things work on a boat. Here is what daily life aboard your shared luxury catamaran looks like. Space: Yacht cabins are smaller than hotel rooms, but they’re just as well-appointed. item.title: Discover Nautilus Sailing’s Learn to Sail Adventures
item.description: We’re excited about our new partnership with Nautilus Sailing , where you can learn to sail on a live aboard course at any of our destinations worldwide. Tim Geisler, lead sailing instructor, has given us the lowdown on Nautilus Sailing and what they offer. “Explore. Dream. Discover. ” The ocean, that expanse of adventure, has always drawn me to itself. Each time I weigh anchor I’m struck by the joy of the sea and the endless possibilities it presents. Those three words from Mark Twain, “Explore. Dream. Discover.” are embodied when I’m on the water. It is this passion for sailing and exploration that has led us to share that unique feeling with others, resulting in the birth of Nautilus Sailing in 2010. Now, nearly 10 years later, we’ve helped thousands of people embark on their own sailing journeys with our live aboard courses, and earn their American Sailing Association certifications. This year we are proud to team up with Dream Yacht Charter as their Official Sailing School! A live aboard sailing course allows students to combine the vacation of a lifetime with a comprehensive sailing course. At Nautilus Sailing we offer trips on modern catamarans and monohulls, in exotic destinations such as the Sea of Cortez (Mexico) , Grenadines (Caribbean) , Tahiti and Mallorca (Spain) , where you can explore a stunning cruising destination, and learn to sail through our accredited program with top notch instructors. These live aboard sailing courses are a fantastic balance between intensive learning, and fun adventures. We are usually busy from 8am to 3pm each day digging in to theory, learning how to operate the boat, and practicing sailing and boat handling skills. We have over 100 practical skills that we have to check each student off on, so there is plenty of action! However, we have a lot of fun in the process as we are constantly on the move sailing between islands. Once the anchor goes down, we love snorkeling, paddle boarding, exploring deserted beaches, going ashore for a rum punch, or just relaxing. So whether you are traveling solo, or with a friend or partner, you can join one of our award-winning live aboard courses, that accept a maximum of 4 students onboard. If you have family or friends, Nautilus can customize a private trip for your group, at any of Dream Yacht Charter’s 60+ global destinations , on the boat of your choosing! We are REALLY excited to be able to offer this unique opportunity. Nautilus Sailing’s live aboard sailing courses start from $3875 per person, depending on the location and type of vessel. These prices are all-inclusive and include your private cabin onboard, all sailing materials and textbooks, formal sailing certification through the American Sailing Association , and 3 meals a day on the boat (apart from 3 evening meals ashore). This investment in your sailing journey will help you gain the skills, experience and confidence to embark on your sailing journey. Learning to sail is then just the first step! Nautilus then encourages their students to take advantage of exclusive discounts with Dream Yacht Charter to start bareboat chartering at one of their bases around the world, and begin building sailing experience as captain of their own vessel. Once students complete a sailing course with Nautilus they become part of the Nautilus Alumni Family, and have access to group flotillas and sailing adventures around the world. In 2019 we had flotillas in Corsica and Greece, a dive trip through the Grenadines, offshore sailing trips in Mexico, and a delivery from Croatia to the Caribbean! Check out all the exciting upcoming opportunities for alumni. “My daughter and I had a wonderful experience with Nautilus in Grenada in January. Six days and nights learning the finer points of sailing in the beautiful waters of Grenada and neighboring islands. Instructor Shaun Tarr was a terrific coach who pushed us to get the most from our experience. We worked hard, got tons of hands-on experience and had a terrif…

item.title: Beware of Posidonia seagrass meadows!
item.description: You are going to be sailing in areas where there are Posidonia seagrass meadows. We urge you to be extremely vigilant. These meadows form crucial underwater ecosystems in the Mediterranean, but they are fragile and threatened by a number of human activities, in particular anchoring of recreational craft. An underwater plant of the Mediterranean Posidonia ( Posidonia oceanica ) is a unique marine plant that’s endemic to the Mediterranean Sea. It is not a seaweed but a true flowering plant, with roots, stems, leaves and flowers. You’ll recognise it by its long, green, ribbon-shaped leaves. Posidonia grows in meadows, forming vast underwater prairies. It reproduces mainly by rhizomes and sometimes by seeds. Posidonia meadows are found in the shallow coastal waters of the Mediterranean, from a depth of 1 to around 40 metres, in clear, well-lit waters. These meadows are particularly abundant in sheltered bays where conditions of temperature, salinity and light are ideal for their growth. Practically the whole of the Mediterranean coastline is involved here: the shores of France, Italy, Croatia, Greece, Spain, Turkey, Tunisia, and more. An essential ecological role Posidonia seagrass meadows provide a habitat and a source of food for a multitude of marine species, including fish, molluscs and crustaceans. They are also ideal spawning grounds and nurseries for young fish. Like real underwater forests, seagrass beds act as carbon sinks, helping to combat climate change: they can store up to 300 tonnes of carbon per hectare. That’s 3 to 5 times more than tropical forests, and this, over hundreds of thousands of hectares. And not to mention their contribution to the production of oxygen, the protection of coasts by attenuating the impact of waves, the preservation of beaches where it accumulates in banks, etc. The loss of these meadows would have serious ecological and economic consequences for the Mediterranean. A protected species under threat Despite their importance, Posidonia meadows are extremely fragile and are threatened by a number of human activities. Boat anchoring, pollution, coastal urbanisation, trawling and climate change are all factors that contribute to their degradation. Seagrass beds are particularly sensitive to anchoring by boats: anchors can uproot these plants and create almost irreparable ‘scars’ in Posidonia meadows, as Posidonia rhizomes grow very slowly (a rate of just 1 cm per year).The presence of these meadows dates back between 60 and 100 million years, when terrestrial flowering plants , which resembled the rushes plant family of today, returned to the marine environment where their distant ancestors came from. Don’t be the one to destroy this extraordinary heritage in a matter of minutes. Please note: Posidonia has been a protected species throughout the Mediterranean since 1995 and is classed as a habitat of European interest. Ensure you are aware of the regulations in force! As a boater, you have a key role to play in protecting Posidonia meadows. Here are a few measures you can take to minimise your impact: 1. Before setting off, consult the maps that indicate the presence of Posidonia meadows. There are several free apps that can help you, such as Nav&Co or Donia. Download them. 2. Don’t anchor in Posidonia meadows: opt for sandy bottoms or consider picking up a mooring buoy whenever possible. 3. Respect protected areas: some regions have marine protected areas where anchoring and other activities are regulated to protect the seagrass meadows. 4. In all cases, adapt your anchoring technique: to avoid scraping the seabed, you must take care to bring your anchor back up in line with the boat, even if you are on sand. 5. Avoid generating any pollution at sea. 6. Share with others: not all boaters are aware of the importance of Posidonia seagrass meadows. And set an example! By adopting these practices, you’ll be helping to preserve Posidonia seagrass meadows and the health of Mediterranean marine ecosy…
